articles.title: Russia’s New Plan to Kill the Armenia-Azerbaijan TRIPP Corridor - The National Interest
articles.summary: Russia’s New Plan to Kill the Armenia-Azerbaijan TRIPP Corridor  The National Interest
articles.full_text:
After its preferred candidates lost election in Armenia earlier this year, Russia is implementing a new strategy against the trans-Caucasian economic corridor: whipping up fears of international conflict.
Having failed in their attempt to unseat Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan in June, Russia’s allies in Armenia have turned their fire on the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), the US-developed transit corridor passing through southern Armenia at the center of last year’s peace deal with Azerbaijan. Throughout September, pro-Russian parties, Kremlin-linked analysts, and revanchist nationalists in the country have worked from a common script: brand the project as Israeli, call on Iran to stop it, and convince the Armenian public that the corridor will cost them their sovereignty
This campaign is unlikely to derail TRIPP this year. Instead, it is aimed at the constitutional referendum Armenia must hold before the peace treaty can be signed. Washington should move faster than it can mature.
Is Iran Planning to Attack the TRIPP Corridor? Iran Doesn’t Think So
The Israeli label is the newest line of attack. On September 18, former Armenian prime minister Khosrov Harutyunyan wrote in the pro-Russian newspaper Golos Armenii that TRIPP bears an “Israeli trace”—describing the corridor as a plan conceived in Israel and merely presented as American, and suggesting that talk of it began at the height of the confrontation among Iran, Israel, and the United States. Historian Armen Ayvazyan has described Azerbaijan’s government as fully dependent on the United States, the United Kingdom, and Israel, implying that Armenia’s would head in a similar direction if the TRIPP were left intact. The security analyst Hrachya Arzumanyan went further on Telegram, alleging that “world Jewry” had been collectively responsible for Armenia’s loss of Nagorno-Karabakh to Azerbaijan in 2023 and vowing to remind them of it “for the next two thousand years.” The label turns a 42-kilometer road and rail line into a front in the Iran war, which makes Tehran a party to it and discredits the project with anyone hostile to Israel.
Iran is the constituency this campaign most wants to mobilize. Vigen Akopyan, the managing partner of the Russian news agency EADaily, wrote on September 22 that the US and Israel had been trying to seal Iran off from every direction, and that TRIPP would turn Armenia’s southern Syunik province into a battleground between Washington and Tehran. Tigran Torosyan, a former speaker of parliament, called the route an American base under another name, one Iran “cannot allow.” Ayvazyan likewise declared Syunik Iran’s “red line,” and Sergey Melkonyan of the Applied Policy Research Institute (APRI) in Armenia suggested Tehran could respond as it did in March, when Iranian drones struck Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan exclave. Indeed, former Iranian foreign minister Ali Akbar Velayati warned in August 2025 that the route would become a graveyard for “Trump’s mercenaries.”
Yet Iran has not made a credible threat to the TRIPP project. Its ambassador in Yerevan, Khalil Shirgholami, has distinguished TRIPP from the Azerbaijani corridor concept Iran long opposed and says Tehran has no reason to object absent a foreign security or military presence. Iran also has few resources with which to act against Armenia; it is under US naval blockade, its oil exports have all but stopped, and its airlines have been barred from Azerbaijan under new US aviation sanctions since late September. The revanchists in Yerevan are trying to draw red lines that Tehran itself does not appear committed to.
How Russia Has Stoked Anti-TRIPP Activism
The domestic message is loss of sovereignty. Gohar Meloyan of Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia party claims 74 percent of the route’s revenue will go to America. The reality is more complicated; the framework Washington and Yerevan announced in January gives the United States a 74 percent stake in a joint development company for an initial 49 years, but the route runs under Armenian law.
This subtlety has been lost in the commentary surrounding the route. Ruben Melkonyan, dean of oriental studies at Yerevan State University, has called TRIPP a road Armenia will host but never control. Levon Zurabyan of the Armenian National Congress, the party of former President Levon Ter-Petrosyan and once the most pragmatic voice on Azerbaijan in Armenian politics, warned it would provoke a proxy war. The analyst Vahe Davtyan implausibly claimed that the corridor had set Armenia against the European Union—even as Brussels has committed €10 billion ($11.2 billion) to the same Middle Corridor TRIPP will feed. Akopyan states the conclusion outright: Armenia can survive only in alliance with Russia and in strategic dialogue with Iran.
It is impossible to miss Russia’s ties to the anti-TRIPP narrative. These voices appear regularly on Russian-owned or Russian-aligned outlets such as EADaily, Sputnik Armenia, 168.am, and Golos Armenii, and they build on a state campaign. Before the June election, independent analysts claimed that in the run-up to Armenia’s elections, the Russian-backed “Matryoshka” propaganda network had published 343 fake videos by early May. The previous year, the Storm-1516 propaganda operation targeted Armenia more than any other country in the world. Moscow has used blunt instruments of coercion as well, threatening to cancel the agreement under which it supplies Armenia’s gas; the members of the Eurasian Economic Union will also convene in December to discuss suspending Armenia’s membership.
A second front has opened in Washington, where Armenian lobbying efforts to enforce human rights sanctions against Azerbaijan may torpedo the peace process. On September 14 and 15, the Armenian National Committee of America held more than 150 meetings on Capitol Hill, pressing lawmakers to enforce Section 907 of the Freedom Support Act and to sign a letter opposing the administration’s extension of its waiver. There is no reason to believe that this effort is coordinated with Moscow. Even so, cutting assistance to Azerbaijan and reviving a 1992 sanction would strip away the leverage that brought Baku to the table, and endanger an enduring peace agreement.
Russia Is Losing the TRIPP Battle—but It Will Have More Chances
For now, this campaign is losing. Pashinyan’s Civil Contract party won 49.8 percent of the vote in June—just shy of an outright majority, but far surpassing Strong Armenia’s 23.3 percent, despite one of the largest Russian influence operations on record. Russia is tied down in Ukraine, and Iran is under blockade. On September 23, representatives of more than 40 companies came to New York to look at TRIPP, accompanied by Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, Sen. Steve Daines (R-MT), and representatives from Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and all five “C5” Central Asian nations. The administration has put $201 million into a Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund.
Pashinyan has held through all of it, and he will probably hold again. His voters are the softer target. Three decades of conflict left the two societies with no trust to spend, and a claim repeated into that vacuum for eighteen months could change public opinion, forcing a shift in policy.
The danger to TRIPP lies in the future timeframe. Azerbaijan will not sign the peace treaty until Armenia removes its territorial claim to Nagorno-Karabakh from its constitution. Armenian voters will need to approve that change in a referendum expected in 2027. Meanwhile, the feasibility study for the route is not due until the end of this year or early next, and the joint development company has yet to be formally launched. Every claim now in circulation, from the Israeli plot to the Iranian red line to the foreign base in Syunik, is an argument for voting no. It will carry more weight if Russia and Iran have recovered some of their strength by then.
Washington can do much to close this gap. It should formally launch the development company and name its leadership, and begin visible work and hiring in Syunik before the referendum, so that voters judge the route by jobs rather than rumors.
Russia and Iran are weaker today than they have been in a generation, and both will recover. The United States should hope that the road is under construction—and the permanent peace treaty signed—before they do.

Joseph Epstein is the director of the Turan Research Center, a senior fellow at the Yorktown Institute, an expert at the N7 Foundation, and a research fellow at the Begin Sadat Center for Strategic Studies at Bar Ilan University. He also sits on the advisory board of the Alekain Foundation, a nonprofit dedicated to providing education to women and girls in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan. articles.title: Putin tells Iran Russia will ‘do everything’ to help end Middle East war - Malay Mail
articles.summary: Putin tells Iran Russia will ‘do everything’ to help end Middle East war  Malay Mail
articles.full_text:
ASHGABAT, Oct 9 — Russia’s President Vladimir Putin vowed yesterday to “do everything” to help end the Middle East war when he met Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian for talks ahead of a regional summit, Russian media reported.
The leaders of two of the world’s most sanctioned nations met after arriving in Turkmenistan for a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) that starts today in the Caspian Sea resort of Avaza.
“We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation,” said Putin. He added that Iran had made “real efforts to end the war” since US-Israeli attacks started on February 28, according to Russian news agencies.
Putin also noted the “positive evolution” in Iran-Russia relations.
The two countries have reinforced diplomatic and military links since Russia launched its offensive in Ukraine in February 2022, becoming increasingly reliant on each other.
Conflict impasse
Ukraine and Western countries have accused Iran of supplying Russia with Shahed drones and short-range missiles for use in the Ukraine war. Russia has been accused of supplying data to Iran for its attacks on US targets in the Middle East.
Putin and Pezeshkian also met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan last month. And in a call on Wednesday, Putin also told Pezeshkian that he was ready to help mediate in the Middle East war, Iranian state news agency IRNA reported.
The contacts came with Iran-US talks at an apparent impasse. Pezeshkian said this week that negotiations with Washington were “meaningless”.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the Russia’s offensive in Ukraine also appear deadlocked, even as both sides intensify attacks.
Putin and Pezeshkian will attend the summit of the CIS — originally a grouping of former Soviet nations — with leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Turkmenistan and other Central Asia states.
The Putin-Pezeshkian meeting was one of several bilateral encounters scheduled on the sidelines of the summit, according to Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov.
Sphere of influence
The CIS was established in 1991 to ease the pain of the Soviet collapse and maintain ties among its former republics.
Some states have left — Georgia withdrew following a 2008 war with Russia, Ukraine halted its participation after Moscow’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and Moldova left in 2023 as it sought closer ties with the European Union.
For Russia, which has found itself isolated since launching the Ukraine conflict in 2022, the CIS proves that it “actually has the orbit and that it has its own sphere of influence that is fortified and institutionalised”, Temur Umarov, a researcher at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre in Berlin, told AFP.
But today’s meeting also comes at a time when several CIS members are seeking to diversify their economic and diplomatic partnerships, notably by strengthening ties with China and Western nations.
“Even if Russia decides to use this platform to propagate anti-Western or anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, that does not mean the other members will automatically subscribe to its position,” Zhanibek Arynov, a Kazakhstan-based researcher specialising in Central Asian geopolitics, told AFP. — AFP

articles.title: Transport is one of the main areas of cooperation between the states of Central Asia and Azerbaijan - President Ilham Aliyev - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Transport is one of the main areas of cooperation between the states of Central Asia and Azerbaijan - President Ilham Aliyev  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
TURKMENBASHI, Turkmenistan, October 8. Transport is one of the primary areas of cooperation between Central Asia and Azerbaijan, President Ilham Aliyev said as he addressed the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Central Asia in Turkmenbashi, Trend's special correspondent reports.
“The Caspian Sea plays an increasingly vital role today in the transport interaction of our countries. The transport infrastructure on both shores of the Caspian is of key importance for connecting Central Asia with Azerbaijan and further onward to international markets,” the head of state emphasized.
The President noted that significant growth in cargo transit volumes across the Caspian is currently being observed. “Our common task is to make these routes more efficient and competitive,” the Azerbaijani leader added.
The 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Azerbaijan and Central Asian countries was held on October 8, 2026, at the Awaza National Tourism Zone in Turkmenbashi, Turkmenistan. It was the first full-fledged meeting in the renewed format following the decision to grant Azerbaijan full participation, adopted at the summit in Tashkent in November 2025.
The meeting addressed regional security, political and diplomatic cooperation, trade and economic ties, energy, transport and logistics corridors, environmental issues and humanitarian cooperation.
The summit resulted in the signing of the Joint Statement of the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Azerbaijan and Central Asian countries, as well as the Decision on the regulatory documents of the format.

articles.title: Uzbekistan, Switzerland explore new projects in energy, mining - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Uzbekistan, Switzerland explore new projects in energy, mining  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Uzbekistan and Switzerland discussed expanding trade, economic and investment cooperation and advancing new joint projects in pharmaceuticals, industry, energy, geology and mining during a meeting in Tashkent on Oct. 6.
This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade of Uzbekistan, following a meeting between Uzbek Investment, Industry and Trade Minister Laziz Kudratov and Simone Giger, the Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Swiss Confederation to the Republic of Uzbekistan.
The sides reviewed prospects for expanding bilateral economic cooperation and implementing new joint investment projects across several sectors, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.
The discussions covered pharmaceuticals, industrial production, energy, geological exploration and mining, as well as the food industry. The parties considered opportunities for developing practical cooperation in these areas and expanding the participation of businesses from both countries in joint projects.
“During the meeting, the parties discussed the prospects for expanding trade and economic cooperation and investment, as well as the implementation of new joint projects,” the ministry said.
Moreover, the sides discussed preparations for the upcoming meeting of the Uzbek-Swiss Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Investment Cooperation. The commission is expected to provide a platform for reviewing bilateral economic ties and identifying new areas for trade and investment cooperation.
Another issue on the agenda was the organization of the “Days of Switzerland” in Uzbekistan, which is intended to support greater interaction and contacts between the two countries.
The meeting concluded with the sides reaffirming their readiness to strengthen the Uzbek-Swiss economic partnership and develop practical cooperation through new projects and expanded business ties.

articles.title: US sanctions 17 ships in push to shut down Iran’s shadow fleet - Iran International
articles.summary: US sanctions 17 ships in push to shut down Iran’s shadow fleet  Iran International
articles.full_text:
The US Treasury sanctioned 17 vessels and their owners Thursday under Operation Economic Outcast, saying the action effectively neutralizes most of Iran’s remaining shadow fleet.
In a statement, Treasury said the ships had carried millions of barrels of Iranian crude, petroleum products and petrochemicals to markets in South and East Asia. The network spanned more than a dozen jurisdictions and relied on international front companies.
Thursday’s broader Iran-related sanctions targeted six individuals, 27 entities and 22 vessels in total, including the 17 ships highlighted by Treasury. The additional targets included five Indian nationals and a Turkish national, along with companies including India’s Samudra Marine Services and SSPL Solutions and the UAE’s Hessonite Ship Management.
“Treasury is starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “No enabler of Iranian sanctions evasion is safe from the full force of Treasury’s authorities.”
Among the targets were the Cameroon-flagged Shenzhen, which Treasury said had transported more than 3.5 million barrels of Iranian crude since November 2025, and the Vanuatu-flagged Tina 5, which carried more than 1.5 million barrels in August. Designated companies include firms in China, Hong Kong, the Marshall Islands and the British Virgin Islands.
Treasury said vessels regularly enter and leave the network, and pledged to continue monitoring attempts to evade sanctions.
Thursday’s measures, issued under Executive Order 13902, freeze the targets’ assets under US jurisdiction and generally prohibit US persons from dealing with them. Foreign financial institutions risk secondary sanctions for knowingly facilitating significant transactions for designated parties.
Treasury also removed the Hakuna Matata and Pinocchio from its sanctions list after they left Iran’s shadow fleet and were sold to non-sanctioned, US-aligned operators. Both vessels had been listed in June 2025.
Launched on August 24 and dubbed Economic D-Day, Operation Economic Outcast seeks to isolate Iran’s revenue and financial networks by increasing pressure on foreign companies and governments that sustain trade with Tehran.
The campaign expanded sanctions exposure across digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, threatening foreign businesses with exclusion from the US financial system. The broader authorities do not automatically sanction every foreign business in those sectors, but allow Washington to designate additional targets.
On October 1, Washington widened the campaign to Iran’s automotive and rail industries, sanctioning major manufacturers including Iran Khodro and SAIPA.
Treasury said the US military blockade, dwindling oil shipments outside it and widening sanctions were leaving Tehran with fewer options to stabilize its economy.
Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said Tuesday that the economy was still functioning and rejected what he described as US predictions of collapse.

articles.title: After The War, A Wider Strategic Space Awaits China And Pakistan - The Friday Times
articles.summary: After The War, A Wider Strategic Space Awaits China And Pakistan  The Friday Times
articles.full_text:
The Iran war is not over; it has entered an even more dangerous phase. The opening of the Houthi front has widened the conflict towards Yemen and the Red Sea, while attacks on Saudi Arabia have activated the Makkah Pact and drawn Pakistan more directly into Gulf security. With both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb under pressure, what began as a conflict centred on Iran has become a wider struggle over regional security, energy flows and some of the world’s most important maritime routes.
Pakistan’s role has consequently evolved from mediation and crisis diplomacy towards a more consequential security role in the Arab Gulf, even as it continues to favour an eventual negotiated settlement. China has consistently supported Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts while seeking to protect its enormous energy, trade and investment interests across the Middle East. Their roles are different, but their strategic priorities increasingly converge—on regional stability, secure sea lanes and economic connectivity—potentially opening a much wider space for China-Pakistan cooperation after the war.
I had an opportunity to examine this changing relationship closely during a 10-day visit to China in September. On September 3, I presented a paper, “China-Pakistan Collaboration in the Iran Conflict: Assessment and Post-Conflict Scenarios,” at an international conference organised by the Pakistan Study Centre at Peking University to mark 75 years of Pakistan-China relations. The gathering brought together scholars and policy practitioners, including former Pakistani foreign secretaries and ambassadors who had served in Beijing.
A week later, on September 11, I attended another conference at the Pakistan Study Centre of Fudan University in Shanghai, bringing together contributors to a forthcoming volume on 75 years of Pakistan-China relations, in which an expanded version of my paper will appear as a chapter. Spending nearly two weeks in China also provided an opportunity to gauge Chinese perceptions at a particularly consequential moment in the relationship.
What struck me was not simply the familiar Chinese confidence in Pakistan as an enduring strategic partner. There was also an appreciation that Pakistan’s relevance is no longer confined to South Asia. The Iran war has brought into sharper focus a geographical reality that CPEC had already begun to reveal: Pakistan sits at the intersection of South Asia, Central Asia, Iran and the Arab Gulf, while China’s economic and political interests now extend deeply across all these regions.
Wars are perhaps the most severe test of strategic partnerships. China and Pakistan have enjoyed exceptionally close relations for decades, sustained by historical trust and remarkably consistent alignment on their principal strategic interests. The Iran conflict has tested that relationship outside its traditional geographical setting and, in doing so, has revealed possibilities that extend well beyond the immediate crisis.
Pakistan entered the conflict in an extraordinarily difficult position. Iran is an immediate neighbour; Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states are vital economic and strategic partners; the United States remains an important relationship; and China is Pakistan’s principal long-term strategic partner. Islamabad could neither afford a prolonged regional war nor choose one relationship at the expense of the others. Its response combined strategic restraint with active diplomacy. Pakistan maintained its channel with Tehran, coordinated closely with Riyadh and other Gulf capitals, remained engaged with Washington and consulted regularly with Beijing. This unusual access across competing centres of power ultimately gave Islamabad the diplomatic space to mediate.
China stood firmly behind that effort. Beijing’s role differed from Pakistan’s, but their principal objective was substantially the same: contain the conflict, prevent its regionalisation and create conditions for a return to diplomacy. The two countries were therefore not necessarily following identical policies, but they were pursuing compatible strategic outcomes.
On March 31, Foreign Ministers Wang Yi and Ishaq Dar announced a joint Five-Point Initiative in Beijing calling for cessation of hostilities, negotiations, respect for sovereignty and regional stability. Its essential principles subsequently found expression in the diplomatic process pursued through Islamabad. Beijing repeatedly praised Pakistan’s mediation, describing its approach as “fair and balanced,” Pakistan as a “reliable and qualified mediator,” and its role in achieving the first-phase US-Iran understanding as “indispensable.”
 Pakistan’s ability to maintain relationships with Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United States and China simultaneously has given Islamabad unusual diplomatic space and increased its relevance to regional security.
There was important historical continuity in this convergence. China has generally preferred diplomacy to military involvement in the Middle East, with its most consequential recent diplomatic achievement in the region coming in 2023, when Beijing facilitated the restoration of relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran after years of hostility. During the present conflict, China again chose diplomatic engagement rather than becoming a military protagonist.
Pakistan’s objective was similarly straightforward. Islamabad did not seek an Iranian or American victory; it sought an end to a war threatening its western neighbourhood, its Gulf partners, its energy security and its economic interests. This alignment of interests, rather than identical policies, explains the close China-Pakistan coordination during the crisis.
The Strait of Hormuz illustrates this convergence most clearly. For Pakistan, disruption of Hormuz means higher energy costs, pressure on foreign exchange, interruption of trade and instability close to its borders. For China, the stakes are even larger because of its enormous dependence on imported Gulf oil and gas and the importance of uninterrupted maritime commerce to its economy.
China’s primary concern in the Gulf is therefore stability: secure energy supplies, freedom of navigation, functioning trade routes and an environment in which commerce and investment can flourish. Beijing has little interest in turning the Middle East into another theatre of great-power confrontation, particularly when geopolitical competition threatens the economic relationships it has painstakingly developed across the region.
This also places the American role in a more nuanced context. China does not necessarily need to replace the United States as the principal external security provider in the Gulf. An American security presence that ensures freedom of navigation through Hormuz and other critical sea lanes can also protect Chinese commercial interests; Beijing’s concern arises when military power becomes an instrument of geopolitical competition that destabilises the region or threatens energy flows.
Pakistan can operate comfortably within this space. Its improving relationship with Washington has not come at the expense of Beijing, while its longstanding relationships with Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf are increasingly acquiring a security dimension alongside their traditional political and economic foundations. This gives Pakistan room to engage multiple major powers without turning its relationships into mutually exclusive choices.
The Makkah Pact with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye is the most important manifestation of this development. Combined with Pakistan’s longstanding bilateral defence relationship with Saudi Arabia, it potentially gives Islamabad a more institutionalised role in Gulf security than it possessed before the Iran conflict. The significance extends beyond immediate defence commitments, because Pakistan is beginning to move from being primarily a bilateral security partner of individual Gulf states towards participation in a broader regional security framework.
If this process consolidates after the war, Pakistan’s strategic relevance in the Middle East will increase substantially. That matters for China because Beijing has spent the past decade developing an enormous economic presence across precisely the same geographical space in which Pakistan’s diplomatic and security role is now growing.
China is already a principal trading partner of the Gulf states, their largest energy customer in Asia and an increasingly important source of investment, infrastructure and technology. Saudi Arabia and the UAE, in particular, have developed extensive economic relationships with Beijing while retaining their longstanding security relationships with Washington. China’s Belt and Road Initiative has reinforced this expansion through infrastructure, energy, logistics and investment projects across the wider region.
 CPEC and Gwadar could evolve from a predominantly bilateral China-Pakistan project into part of a broader transregional network linking western China and Pakistan with Iran, Central Asia and the Gulf.
Pakistan is approaching the same region from another direction. It brings geography, military capability, longstanding relations with Arab states and, after its role in the Iran crisis, greater diplomatic credibility. China brings capital, technology, markets and enormous economic stakes, creating roles that are potentially complementary rather than competitive.
This is also why CPEC should no longer be viewed solely as a bilateral Pakistan-China undertaking. Sadyr Japarov spoke at the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan
President of the Kyrgyz Republic Sadyr Japarov participated on October 8 in the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, which is taking place at the "Avaza" complex. During the meeting, he delivered a speech in which he outlined key directions for further cooperation among the countries in the region.
The head of state emphasized the need for developing industrial cooperation, proposing that the governments of the countries identify specific projects in the areas of agricultural product processing and light industry, as well as in the production of construction materials and logistics. It is important to specify the participants, sources of funding, and timelines for implementing these initiatives.
The president also highlighted the development of e-commerce as a separate direction. He proposed creating a unified e-commerce platform for Central Asia and Azerbaijan, which would provide businesses and consumers access to regional products and create opportunities for their promotion.
Sadyr Japarov stressed that the development of e-commerce requires the formation of logistics infrastructure, including delivery, warehousing, and customs clearance. Kyrgyzstan is ready to involve specialists from the High Technology Park to implement this initiative.
The president noted the importance of reliable transport routes for effective economic cooperation. He emphasized the construction of the "China – Kyrgyzstan – Uzbekistan" railway, which will create new opportunities for integrating the countries of the region into international transport and production connections.
"Our benchmark should be measurable results: reducing delivery costs and shortening travel time. Each country should have the opportunity to participate in transport projects and reap economic benefits from them," the head of state stated.
Additionally, Sadyr Japarov emphasized the need to preserve glaciers and mountain ecosystems, which are linked to the long-term sustainable development of the region. He highlighted the importance of rational use of natural resources and the application of innovations for future generations.
The president also pointed out the opportunities for bringing peoples closer together through the formation of a common tourist space, stating that the countries possess complementary tourism potential. He proposed developing cooperation based on the principle of "one trip - several countries."
In conclusion, the president emphasized Kyrgyzstan's readiness to continue contributing to strengthening good neighborliness and developing mutually beneficial cooperation to ensure sustainable economic growth and improve the well-being of the peoples of the region.

TURKMENBASHI, Turkmenistan, October 8. Azerbaijan's chairmanship of the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asian countries will give additional impetus to the format, President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev said on October 8 at the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan in Awaza Complex, Trend’s special correspondent reports.
“I am convinced that under the leadership of the Azerbaijani side, our work within this format will receive additional impetus, while brotherly cooperation will contribute to strengthening unity, trust and solidarity,” he said.
Mirziyoyev noted that the Consultative Meeting of Central Asian countries with the participation of Azerbaijan is of historical significance.
“Today's meeting is of particular importance as it is being held for the first time together with brotherly Azerbaijan,” he said.
Mirziyoyev also highlighted Turkmenistan's successful chairmanship.
“Over the past year, we have made significant progress in regional cooperation on many important issues and reached concrete agreements. Central Asia has changed significantly in recent years. The very atmosphere of relations between our countries has changed. We meet more often, discuss issues openly, find solutions and support each other. Our Consultative Meetings have played an important role in this.
When creating this format, we proceeded from a simple understanding: the prosperity and security of Central Asia directly depend on trust between our states. A historic event was the completion of the procedure for concluding the Treaty of Friendship, Good Neighborliness and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century.
At the same time, we are not seeking to create cumbersome structures. We need a flexible and clear format in which strong, sovereign and independent states cooperate on the basis of mutual respect, trust and pragmatism. This approach has already produced results,” he said.
Mirziyoyev also proposed stepping up efforts to establish a regional alliance on critical minerals initiated by Uzbekistan. According to him, one of the first steps could be the creation of a unified digital map of critical mineral reserves in Central Asia.
He noted that such a resource would provide a more comprehensive picture of the region's potential and demonstrate to international investors that the Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan are ready to develop this area jointly.
“The next major area is technological development. Artificial intelligence and big data are already transforming industry, transport, energy, agriculture, education and public administration. The productivity of our economies and our ability to compete in the future will largely depend on these technologies. At the same time, digital projects often deliver results faster than large-scale infrastructure projects. Therefore, I propose that we combine the capabilities of our countries and begin creating shared computing infrastructure.
Its foundation could be an interconnected network of national data centers. This would allow us to use computing capacity more efficiently, develop our own digital products and create conditions for large-scale artificial intelligence projects. But infrastructure alone is not enough. We also need specialists, research and strong technology companies. Therefore, we propose launching joint targeted training programs, supporting research projects and creating more opportunities for technology entrepreneurship.
Finally, one of the most important issues for the future of our region is people. Our country has significant demographic potential. The population is growing, and the number of young people is increasing. Our future will largely depend on the quality of their education and professional training: what our economy will look like in 10, 20 or 30 years. We must keep this in mind. Therefore, education and youth support should have a special place in our cooperation. We need to better understand what specialists our economies will need tomorrow.
For this purpose, we propose developing a regional atlas of in-demand professions and skills. It could combine our countries' forecasts for areas where there is already a shortage of specialists and where demand is expected to grow in the coming years. This would allow universities and vocational institutions to take into account the actual needs of our economies in advance. In the future, we could train specialists for specific major projects being implemented simultaneously in several countries of our region. In this way, education would be directly linked to the development of industry, transport, energy, digital technologies and other sectors.
Esteemed heads of state, we have achieved a great deal in recent years. It is now important to consolidate these changes and make our cooperation sustainable for decades to come. The formula is simple: solidarity and trust for the sake of development and security. We are responsible for the region we leave to future generations. It should be peaceful, secure and economically strong, and provide people with opportunities to live, work, study and raise their children with dignity. Taking this opportunity, I congratulate Azerbaijan on assuming the chairmanship of the Consultative Meetings,” he said.

articles.title: Uzbekistan to rank among Europe and Central Asia’s fastest-growing economies in 2026 — World Bank - Daryo
articles.summary: Uzbekistan to rank among Europe and Central Asia’s fastest-growing economies in 2026 — World Bank  Daryo
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan’s real GDP growth is projected to accelerate from 7.7% in 2025 to 7.9% in 2026, keeping the country among the fastest-growing economies in Europe and Central Asia, according to the World Bank’s latest regional economic outlook.
The World Bank Group’s Europe and Central Asia Economic Update: Making AI Work: Jobs, Firms, and Productivity, released on October 6, projects economic growth across developing countries in Europe and Central Asia to slow to 2.2% in 2026, down from 2.6% in 2025.
The slowdown is expected to reflect higher energy prices, geopolitical tensions, and weaker demand from trading partners. Excluding Russia, which accounts for about 40% of the region’s total output, economic growth is projected to decline from 3.7% in 2025 to 3% in 2026.
Despite the weaker regional outlook, favorable labor market conditions, rising real wages, higher remittances, increased tourist flows, and public investment are supporting economic activity. Temporary government support measures have also partly cushioned the impact of higher energy prices on households and businesses, although they have added pressure to public finances in some countries.
Central Asia remains the fastest-growing subregion
Central Asia is projected to remain the fastest-growing subregion in Europe and Central Asia, with growth expected to reach 5.8% in 2026. Robust domestic demand and continued government investment in transport and energy are expected to drive the expansion.
Kyrgyzstan’s economy is forecast to grow by 9.6%, while Uzbekistan is projected to expand by 7.9%. In Uzbekistan, growth is expected to be supported by resilient domestic demand, strong real wage growth, rising employment, robust remittance inflows, and continued structural reforms.
Remittances to Uzbekistan reached a record $9.2bn in the first half of 2026, up 13% from a year earlier, with Russia accounting for approximately 70% of transfers. Non-gold exports increased by nearly 30%, supported by expanding trade with China and neighboring Central Asian economies.
Elsewhere in Europe and Central Asia, growth in the Western Balkans is projected to accelerate from 2.6% in 2025 to 3.1% in 2026. Poland’s economy is expected to grow by 3.6%, while Ukraine’s growth is forecast at 1.2% amid further damage to critical infrastructure and disruptions to exports.
AI adoption lags behind exposure
The World Bank’s report also examines how artificial intelligence (AI) could help countries increase productivity and create jobs as working-age populations shrink. AI is spreading faster across the region than economies are currently able to absorb it. About one in five workers, predominantly young and highly educated, are employed in occupations meaningfully exposed to AI, while fewer than one in 10 firms currently use the technology, mainly for basic tasks.
The report identifies gaps in foundational education and management skills, integrated data systems, and computing infrastructure as barriers to wider AI adoption.
In Uzbekistan, clerical workers have the highest AI exposure among occupational groups, while practical use of technology remains limited by gaps in foundational digital skills. With its young and growing population, Uzbekistan is among the countries implementing industry-led skills programs aimed at bridging the gap between basic digital proficiency and an AI-ready workforce.
The World Bank noted that the key risk for the region over the next decade may not be excessive AI adoption, but rather insufficient adoption and adaptation to the technology.

articles.title: China’s BRI Cuts Both Ways for Authoritarian Rule - The China-Global South Project
articles.summary: China’s BRI Cuts Both Ways for Authoritarian Rule  The China-Global South Project
articles.full_text:
- Chinese BRI investment can reinforce entrenched authoritarian rule by bolstering patronage networks and developmental legitimacy, exemplified by Cambodia's CPP.
- Chinese investment can fuel corruption scandals, elite fractures and opposition mobilization, as with Najib's projects and Barisan Nasional's defeat in Malaysia.
- Regime outcomes are contingent; BRI's political effects depend on existing political settlements, elite cohesion and contestation strength.
By Neil Loughlin
China’s rise has intensified debate over whether its growing economic influence promotes authoritarianism internationally. Critics have portrayed President Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) as supporting authoritarian partners, weakening democratic pressure and helping construct a more autocratic international order. But while Chinese investment has reinforced authoritarian governments in some cases, it has intensified political conflict and weakened incumbent regimes in others.
Economic and political ties to powerful authoritarian states can provide governments with material support during instability, reinforce patronage networks and reduce the impact of international pressure. Yet the potential for external material investment to destabilize authoritarian regimes has received less attention.
Unequal resource allocation can generate intra-elite tensions, while those excluded from patronage networks or economic opportunities may align with opposition movements. In analyzing how external investment becomes part of existing struggles over power and resources, a key consideration is identifying who benefits from investment and how this aligns with the prevailing political and economic system.
Cambodia and Malaysia illustrate these dynamics because both received Chinese investment after 2013 while their long-ruling electoral authoritarian governments faced serious political crises. Both regimes relied on patronage, clientelism and performance-based legitimacy to sustain ruling coalitions. Chinese investment might have been expected to reinforce incumbent authoritarian rule in both cases. Instead, their political trajectories diverged.
In Cambodia, the closely contested July 2013 election posed the strongest challenge to the Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) in decades. The opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party won almost 45 percent of the vote, while workers, farmers, youth and other groups joined a broader protest movement against CPP rule. The government responded by suppressing dissent, restricting civil society and dissolving the main opposition party through the Supreme Court in 2017, leaving the CPP virtually unopposed in the 2018 election.
Chinese investment expanded during this crisis and entered a political economy dominated by a closely connected state–party apparatus, business tycoons and the security forces. Politically connected Cambodian firms became local partners in Chinese-backed infrastructure, industrial and property projects. These arrangements reinforced existing patronage networks and gave leading economic elites a material interest in the continuation of CPP rule.
Chinese-funded projects also supported the CPP’s claims to developmental legitimacy. Then-prime minister Hun Sen presented infrastructure and economic growth as evidence that political stability produced national progress. Labor mobilization, environmental protests and opposition politics could be portrayed as threats to development. Chinese finance expanded as US and EU critics highlighted the Cambodian government’s repression and threatened sanctions or trade restrictions. Chinese investment helped maintain elite cohesion and reduced the costs of Western pressure.
Malaysia followed a different path. Before 2018, the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition had dominated the country under a system of repressive but competitive electoral authoritarianism. Elections heavily favored the ruling coalition, but opposition parties could compete and mobilize. The political settlement between the BN and its principal party, the United Malays National Organization, was already fragmenting. Its dominance had weakened after the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, the rise of the Reformasi movement and chronic divisions within the ruling elite. Civil society organizations had also developed the capacity to mobilize public dissatisfaction.
Then-prime minister Najib Razak initially appeared to be offered a lifeline by the post-2014 increase in Chinese investment into Malaysia. Large infrastructure projects could generate contracts for government-linked companies, reward political allies and reinforce the coalition’s developmental credentials. But Chinese investment also became embroiled in the political and financial crises that helped end BN’s dominance.
The long-envisioned East Coast Rail Link connecting Kuala Lumpur with cities in the east of Peninsular Malaysia was revived by Najib’s government in 2016 with Chinese financing. The scheme’s budget was alleged to have been inflated partly to help cover debts generated through the misuse of funds from the 1Malaysia Development Berhad state investment vehicle. Other China-linked investment projects, including Johor’s Forest City development, also raised concerns surrounding foreign ownership, sovereignty and the distribution of benefits.
These controversies saw Chinese investment feed into domestic political conflicts that long predated the BRI. Najib sought to use Chinese capital to preserve patronage networks and stabilize his ruling coalition, while his opponents — including Mahathir Mohamad and the Pakatan Harapan opposition bloc — presented the same investments as evidence of corruption, economic mismanagement and threats to national sovereignty.
The opposition’s organization ensured elections remained sufficiently competitive. These grievances contributed to BN’s defeat in May 2018.
Malaysia’s post-2018 governments nevertheless continued to seek access to Chinese investment. Mahathir renegotiated several major BRI projects, while subsequent governments also remained supportive of Malaysia’s involvement in the BRI. The more competitive political environment only altered the struggles over how BRI investment was distributed and controlled.
The contrast in political outcomes linked to BRI investment in Cambodia and Malaysia highlights the need for caution when drawing simplistic conclusions about the authoritarian effects of Chinese investment. BRI investment may reinforce the political status quo where elites maintain stable coalitions and effectively subdue dissent, as seen in Cambodia. Where elite power is fractured, weak, or contested, as it was in Malaysia, outside investment can instead undermine an authoritarian regime if the forces contesting it are strong enough.
Authoritarian outcomes linked to Chinese investment are not inevitable, but largely depend on how such investments interact with existing political settlements and political economy dynamics in recipient states. External investment alone did not determine regime outcomes — instead, it became part of ongoing internal political conflicts, amplifying underlying mechanisms of political control and contestation.
Neil Loughlin is Senior Lecturer in Comparative Politics at City St George’s, University of London. articles.title: Heine Discusses New Volume on China’s Belt and Road Initiative in Quincy Institute Interview - Boston University
articles.summary: Heine Discusses New Volume on China’s Belt and Road Initiative in Quincy Institute Interview  Boston University
articles.full_text:
Jorge Heine, former Research Professor at the Pardee School of Global Studies and current non-resident fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, recently joined Sarang Shidore, director of the Quincy Institute’s Global South program, to discuss Traversing the Belt and Road: The World According to China and China According to the World (Harvard University Press), a forthcoming edited volume, that examines China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) more than a decade after its launch.
Co-edited by Heine, Min Ye, professor of international relations at the Pardee School; Grant Rhode, Wutong Chair Professor at Beijing Language and Culture University; and Andrew Wilson, John A. van Beuren Chair of Asia-Pacific Studies and Professor of Strategy & Policy at the United States Naval War College; the book brings together scholars from around the world to assess the BRI’s impact on development, geopolitics, governance, and great-power competition across Asia, Africa, Europe, and Latin America.
During the conversation, Heine traced the evolution of the BRI from its original vision to its present form, explaining that “what it wanted to do was to recreate the Silk Road, to reconnect East Asia with Europe, and in so doing to recreate Eurasia.” While the BRI’s early years were defined by large-scale infrastructure projects, he argued that the initiative has since adapted, with greater emphasis on green development, digital connectivity, and smaller, more targeted investments. The volume explores these changes while assessing the BRI’s enduring role as one of the world’s most ambitious development programs.
Heine noted that central argument of both the book is that the BRI is not simply imposed by Beijing but shaped by the countries that participate in it. He described Latin America’s engagement with the initiative as a “co-production,” highlighting how governments and local actors have helped define projects and priorities. Drawing on examples ranging from Peru’s Port of Chancay to rail investments in Africa and Southeast Asia, he emphasized the importance of local decision-making and domestic agency in understanding BRI outcomes. He also challenged some conventional narratives about Chinese overseas lending, arguing that cases such as Sri Lanka’s Hambantota International Port are better explained through local political and economic dynamics than through claims of a deliberate Chinese “debt-trap” strategy.
The discussion also addressed the relationship between the BRI and growing U.S.-China competition. Heine argued that Chinese financing has helped address major infrastructure gaps across the Global South and noted that many governments continue to view economic engagement with China as essential to their development strategies. “The economic action in today’s world is not in Europe, is not in North America. It is in Asia,” he observed.
At the same time, he welcomed new initiatives, stating, “The West should compete with China for the developing of infrastructure in Asia, Africa, and Latin America,” he said, “it should not try to exclude China from participating in this.”
In his closing remarks, he suggested that cooperation between China’s technological capabilities and Latin America’s resource base could play an important role in advancing the global green transition, a theme explored throughout Traversing the Belt and Road.
The full book talk can be watched here.
A former research professor at the Frederick S. Pardee School of Global Studies, Jorge Heine is a diplomat, international relations scholar, and lawyer. He is currently a non-resident fellow at the Quincy Institute. He has served as an ambassador of Chile to China, India, and South Africa. Heine has written over fifteen books, including The Non-Aligned World: Striking Out in an Era of Great Power Competition (2025), which provides insights on how the Global South can navigate the changing diplomatic landscape amid the U.S.-China rivalry, and Traversing the Belt and Road: The World According to China and China According to the World (2026).

articles.summary: Beijing Building Massive Bridge In America’s Backyard  The Daily Caller
articles.full_text:
A Chinese construction conglomerate has laid the groundwork for building Latin America’s longest cable-stayed bridge in Brazil by 2031.
The Salvador-Itaparica Bridge will be built via public-private partnership including Chinese Communications Construction and the state-owned China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC), per South China Morning Post. The bridge would grant China access to one of Brazil’s most lucrative international trade flashpoints.
It marks the latest development in the Belt and Road Initiative, (BRI), a Chinese strategy that the State Department has described as an attempt from China to “create economic dependencies and to coerce others.” The BRI involves China investing in the infrastructure of developing countries in the Middle East, Central Asia, Latin America, and Africa. (RELATED: Pentagon Cuba Planning Expands As Army Reserve Surveys Troops For Possible Deployment)
“Brazil is a welcoming environment now for the Chinese, politically and economically…a lot of investment is already there, there’s a huge internal market and many other infrastructure projects have already been done,” Latin American Studies Professor Evan Ellis of the United States Army War College’s Strategic Studies Institute told the South China Morning Post. Brazil is a member of the Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa (BRICS) economic coalition. Comprising of 11 member countries and partner nations, BRICS is a coalition aimed at allowing developing economies to trade without using the American dollar or aligning with western interests.
Brazilian President Lula: China can be our partner, bringing technology to us, and so can the United States. I have no restrictions regarding the United States. But Trump has to understand that he takes care of the United States. I take care of Brazil. https://t.co/MkwOhRMoFM
— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 2, 2026
The Chinese Embassy in Washington told the Daily Caller News Foundation that it’s “not familiar with the specifics.”
The Salvador-Itaparica Bridge would be part of a wider 29-mile project, the South China Morning Post reports. Containing the Port of Salvador and several private terminals, All Saints Bay serves as a vital hub for foreign trade in Brazil. It is considered a key trading region for products including petrochemicals, fuel oil, nickel, iron and vanadium.
Latin America is a long-term interest for China. It has invested in both a Peruvian port and a 3,000 mile-long rail line in Brazil that could enable trade routes that circumvent the Panama Canal , the DCNF reported last September.
However, the upcoming October 25th presidential run-off election may complicate Brazil’s relationship with Beijing is Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro wins, the South China Morning Post reported. Bolsonaro aims to veer away from China dependency and partner with the U.S., including giving America access to the country’s rare earth minerals.
The Trump administration has renewed American interest in Latin America. On Jan. 3rd, American Special Forces conducted a high-stakes raid ousting Venezuela’s socialist dictator Nicolas Maduro. Meanwhile, America has begun to intercept oil shipments headed for Cuba, aiming to suffocate the regime in Havana.

articles.title: Russian attack on buses in Ukraine’s Kramatorsk kills at least 30 people - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Russian attack on buses in Ukraine’s Kramatorsk kills at least 30 people  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
A Russian attack on two buses has killed at least 30 people and wounded 18 others in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk, near the front line, authorities said.
The local prosecutor’s office on Thursday posted photos of bodies and debris strewn across a road in front of the burning metal shell of a bus.
Police said the attack took place on a street where two city buses were operating at the time. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike hit a bus stop and that Ukraine would respond.
“This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is attempting to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world must respond … firmly,” he said on Telegram.
The Donetsk governor accused Russia of “deliberately targeting civilians”.
“For them [the Russians], a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible,” Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram.
Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb.
‘More and more dangerous’
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said glide bombs “do not have the precision of a ballistic missile or the first-person view of something like a drone, so they don’t have the same accuracy as those weapons”.
There was no way of knowing whether these buses were intentionally targeted or if they were “at the wrong place at the wrong time”, MacAlpine said.
The correspondent added this was one of the largest and deadliest aerial attacks in recent months, “in a sign of how the frontline city of Kramatorsk is becoming more and more dangerous”.
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022.
Kramatorsk is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as part of Russia.
It has served as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of Moscow’s war and is part of the so-called “fortress belt” that troops are fighting to hold.
Russian forces have edged close to the city’s eastern edge, which has prompted calls for civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine.
‘No military targets’
Kramatorsk City Council said it was “yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population”.
“Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets,” it added.
Later on Thursday, a drone strike on Kramatorsk killed two more people. A Russian drone struck a civilian car, Kramatorsk City Council said on its Telegram channel, adding that Russian troops also killed three people in the settlement of Bilenke, which borders Kramatorsk.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, the death toll from Wednesday’s Russian missile attack on a residential building in the city of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region rose to 22, including five children, Governor Vyacheslav Chaus said in a statement on Telegram.
President Zelenskyy said a cruise missile directly hit the building in Pryluky, about 150km (93 miles) east of the capital, Kyiv.
In Kyiv, the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said two people were found dead on Thursday after a fire at a four-storey building that was hit by a drone in the densely populated Solomyansky district.
Klitschko has said the attacks, which have hit key transport bridges in the city, as well as the rail network and energy grid, were “tearing Kyiv apart”.
He said four people were killed and 19 others injured in “enemy attacks” in Kyiv on Thursday.
Attack on Russian data centre
Meanwhile, in Russia, a drone caused a fire at a data centre belonging to Russian technology company Yandex, the firm told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
Unverified images posted on social media showed columns of thick, black smoke pouring from the roof of the building, which the company said was in the central Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow.
Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with some of the latest Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
The former head of Ukraine’s Centre for Countering Disinformation said Kyiv was responsible for the strike on the Yandex facility, writing on Telegram: “Two can play at this game.”
The firm is Russia’s largest technology company.
Often dubbed “Russia’s Google”, Yandex runs the country’s most popular search engine and a food-ordering and ride-hailing app used by tens of millions of people across the Russian-speaking world.
Ukraine also claimed to have struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometres (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine’s General Staff described the complex as one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities.
Separately, a man was killed, and a woman was injured in a drone attack on the Moscow region, Andrei Vorobyov, the regional governor, said. A residential building and three cars were damaged in the attack.
In Russia’s Omsk region, Vitaly Khotsenko, the region’s governor, said Kyiv had hit an industrial zone. The Omsk region in Siberia hosts an oil refinery operated by Gazprom Neft.
Ukraine has been waging its own campaign of long-distance drone strikes against military, energy and commercial targets in a bid to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war.
‘Dangerous stalemate’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday said Russia’s war in Ukraine was at a dangerous stalemate and that Washington would keep working towards a settlement to end the conflict.
“We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair. And that’s what we’re committed to continuing to do,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Portugal.
The US official said escalations could spark a wider conflict.
“That escalation could wind up being a sabotage campaign in neighbouring countries that are members of NATO,” he said, adding that other things “could quickly turn what is a war between two countries into a much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict”.
“This war needs to end in a negotiated settlement. The sooner, the better. The United States stands ready to facilitate that. We have tried. We will continue to try. But we’re also not going to invest in pointless processes if we can’t make progress,” Rubio added.
Talks in the US
The remarks came as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner prepare to meet Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday in a fresh attempt to revive efforts to end the war.
Witkoff and Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv last month.
Zelenskyy confirmed the talks, which he said were expected to last two days.
“The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow,” he said on Thursday. “We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group.”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s delegation would include his chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov; the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, Rustem Umerov; the first deputy head of the President’s Office, Sergiy Kyslytsya; and parliamentary faction leader David Arakhamia.
Zelenskyy said last week that Washington wanted to broker a new round of talks between Ukraine and Russia by the end of October.
The Kremlin has said three-way talks involving the US could take place in October. Previous rounds have produced no tangible progress towards peace.

articles.title: The vital link in Central Asia | Gulf Times - Gulf Times
articles.summary: The vital link in Central Asia | Gulf Times  Gulf Times
articles.full_text:
Historically, Central Asia was the vibrant hub of the Great Silk Road, connecting East and West. Following centuries of administrative centralisation, this historical role contracted, but since gaining independence in 1991, Central Asian nations have worked to revive their global connectivity. Situated at the heart of the region, Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries globally. It is also the only nation in Central Asia sharing direct borders with all four neighbouring states and Afghanistan.
For nearly a quarter-century after 1991, this central location was a source of tension due to border disputes, water conflicts, and high tariffs. Furthermore, prior to 2016, Uzbekistan pursued a cautious, self-contained foreign policy, maintaining diplomatic ties with 134 nations and a visa-free regime limited to about 10 CIS states.
Under President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, this approach changed dramatically through pragmatic regional diplomacy and rapid reforms. Tashkent transformed its geographical disadvantage into a logistics asset, expanding diplomatic relations to 168 countries and granting visa-free travel to citizens of over 90 nations. For the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries seeking economic diversification in Eurasia, Uzbekistan has become a logical gateway to the broader
Central Asian economy Thawing Ice in the Region
Between 2017 and 2025, Tashkent fundamentally shifted its regional strategy, resolving long-standing structural bottlenecks across three core areas: border delimitation, transboundary water security, and trade-industrial co-operation. Decades of border friction and complex enclaves in the Fergana Valley were decisively resolved between 2022 and 2023 through intensive diplomacy, successfully finalising borders and reopening long-closed checkpoints.
Simultaneously, transboundary water disputes — such as those concerning Tajikistan’s Rogun Hydropower Plant and the Kampir-Abad reservoir — shifted from opposition to regional co-operation through landmark joint-management agreements that balanced downstream and upstream interests.
These diplomatic breakthroughs catalyzed comprehensive economic opening. By introducing a 30-day visa-free framework, restoring long-severed rail, bus, and transit connections, and dismantling trade barriers, Tashkent accelerated transit connectivity across Central Asia. By 2025, all five Central Asian republics—Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan—began taking synchronised steps toward deeper integration, effectively eliminating the primary layer of geopolitical risk for institutional partners in Riyadh, Doha, or Abu Dhabi.
Building Multi-Directional Trade Corridors
Prior to 2016, Uzbekistan pursued a cautious, self-contained model, but following a strategic shift toward openness, it initiated a comprehensive policy of building multi-directional trade corridors. The Chinese Direction and the Eastern Corridor: Before 2016, bilateral trade with China stood at roughly $4.2bn, limited to raw materials. Through pragmatic diplomacy, China became Uzbekistan’s largest trading partner, with trade tripling to $13–14bn. Total Chinese investment grew from $2.2bn in 2015 to over $15bn by 2025, driving manufacturing, renewable energy, automotive, and infrastructure sectors. By 2024, freight transport reached 6mn tonnes, transforming Uzbekistan into an active transit hub along China–Europe supply routes.
The European Direction (The Middle Corridor)
Previously, trade with the European Union hovered around $2.0–2.3bn under basic 1996 frameworks, with minimal investment. Pragmatic diplomacy reshaped this: Uzbekistan secured EU GSP+ status, allowing over 6,200 product lines duty-free access. Trade grew 2.5-fold to $6bn, with over 1,000 European-capitalised companies operating locally. Relations reached a milestone at the April 2025 EU–Central Asia Summit in Samarkand, elevating the partnership to a strategic level. Under Europe’s €12bn Global Gateway package, Uzbekistan emerged as a key regional hub for the Middle Corridor—bypassing traditional northern routes—and a vital link for Critical Raw Materials.
These shifts demonstrate that under President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Uzbekistan actively redrew Eurasia’s logistical landscape. Transforming from a historically isolated country into an indispensable strategic bridge connecting East, West, North, and South stands as a clear example of modern pragmatic diplomacy.
Gulf–Central Asia Relations
The historic 2023 Jeddah Summit under the C5+GCC format opened a vibrant new chapter in interregional co-operation, culminating in a landmark Joint Declaration and a comprehensive 5-year roadmap spanning politics, security, economics, investment, energy, transport, and cultural-humanitarian affairs. Subsequent high-level investment forums in Tashkent, Riyadh, Doha, and Abu Dhabi successfully translated these political agreements into multi-billion-dollar project portfolios, driving total trade turnover between the GCC and Central Asian nations well past the $10bn threshold.
Beyond conventional trade, the expanding partnership between the Gulf nations and Central Asia spans much deeper economic integration, with Uzbekistan uniquely positioned as the core platform for driving GCC engagement across the region. A primary engine of this collaboration lies in Uzbekistan’s abundant reserves of strategic raw materials. The country holds major global rankings in critical minerals, including substantial reserves of uranium, copper, tungsten, molybdenum, lithium, and rare earth elements (REEs).
Historically, much of this immense resource wealth was exported exclusively as raw materials or basic semi-finished goods. This exact gap creates an exceptional strategic opportunity for Gulf investors. Rather than limiting their involvement to raw extraction, investors can channel capital into local deep-processing capabilities and high-value-added production chains directly inside Uzbekistan:
Advanced Mineral Processing: Transitioning from raw exports to establishing advanced industrial complexes and gigafactories that manufacture critical components for electric vehicles (EVs), renewable energy systems, and advanced battery storage. Similarly, raw uranium can feed into domestic nuclear medicine manufacturing and advanced isotope production, while tungsten and other rare metals can be utilized to produce ultra-light, durable alloys for aviation and heavy industries.
Green Energy Hub: Renewable energy co-operation represents another powerful pillar. Industry giants from the Gulf—such as Saudi Arabia’s ACWA Power, the UAE’s Masdar, and Qatar’s Nebras Power—have become leading foreign investors in Uzbekistan’s energy transformation. With Uzbekistan rapidly expanding its renewable capacity toward ambitious 2030 targets (accounting for a substantial share of total generation), collaboration is extending into large-scale battery energy storage systems, green hydrogen export initiatives, and the localised manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, and turbine parts.
This integration establishes a regional “green energy loop” that cuts production costs by 30% to 50%, ensures full compliance with international standards such as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and directly supports national development blueprints like Saudi Vision 2030, Qatar National Vision 2030, and the UAE Centennial 2071.
Agro-Logistics Hub: Amid growing water scarcity and limited arable land, food security is a top national priority for Gulf states. Uzbekistan’s favourable climate and rich agricultural output position it as an ideal food-security partner. By constructing modern cold-storage facilities, advanced sorting and packaging hubs, enforcing GSO Halal certifications, and securing direct transit corridors, Uzbekistan functions as a regional agro-logistics center that consolidates agricultural output across Central Asia for rapid delivery to Gulf markets.
These multi-dimensional footprints empower Gulf corporations to view Uzbekistan not merely as a standalone domestic market of 38mn people, but as an integrated manufacturing, industrial, and logistics gateway providing seamless access to the wider Central Asian market of over 80 million residents and broader Eurasian economic spaces.
Conclusion
Taken together, these developments reflect Uzbekistan’s foreign policy shift since 2016 from a cautious stance to an open, pragmatic, and diversified approach. Robust economic partnerships with China, the EU, and the Gulf have significantly expanded Tashkent’s diplomatic and economic horizons. Furthermore, Uzbekistan’s geographical position along the Eastern and Middle corridors has turned a historic vulnerability into a strategic advantage. By connecting transport networks across Eurasia, Uzbekistan serves as an indispensable commercial bridge between East, West, North, and South—stimulating cross-border investment, energy collaboration, and infrastructural growth throughout Central Asia.
- The writer, Shohboz Makhammadrizaev, is an independent researcher

articles.full_text:
Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues
The extradition of Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev is not under discussion, and Baku has not made such a request. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists this during his traditional hour-long briefing.
“What extradition are you talking about? There is no such issue, and we are not discussing it. Azerbaijan has made no request,” he said.
At the same time, he stressed that Armenia would have returned Musayev on the same day if he had not committed a crime.
Pashinyan described the Azerbaijani serviceman, who illegally crossed into Armenia and shot a resident of the village of Shaki, as having committed an “ordinary crime”. The prime minister drew parallels with other forms of cross-border crime:
“We also have other cases of cross-border crime. Drugs are constantly exported to Armenia and transported through Armenia in transit. There is no need to turn this into an apocalypse.”
The prime minister does not believe the incident in Shaki could threaten the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.
He considers the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established an achievement that requires protection. He warns that they could destroy it in a day, while reaching the current state of relations could take another 30 years. For this reason, he does not consider it appropriate to make statements that could threaten the peace process.
On 1 October 2026, Nasimi Musayev illegally entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. Local residents found him inside a house, where he opened fire with an assault rifle and wounded a 39-year-old woman. Her three children witnessed the incident. Her two sons also suffered injuries, while her daughter has yet to recover psychologically.
Musayev fled after the shooting, but authorities detained him shortly afterwards in another house. The Armenian Prosecutor’s Office brought criminal charges under five articles of the Criminal Code. The charges include illegally crossing the border, causing serious bodily harm to a local resident and violating the inviolability of a home. A court ordered his detention for two months.
During the briefing, the prime minister also addressed Dmitry Medvedev’s controversial statement about turning Armenia into a “new Ukraine”, a possible meeting with Aliyev at the CIS summit and the issue of missing persons.
- Opinion from Yerevan: Baku steps up pressure on Armenia with new tools
- Azerbaijani soldier enters Armenia, fires at local residents
- ‘Unresolved issues and conflicting narratives remain’ — Pashinyan on relations with Azerbaijan
“No official meetings are planned”: on contacts with Putin and Aliyev
On 8-9 October, Pashinyan will attend the CIS summit in Turkmenistan. Asked about possible meetings with the presidents of Russia and Azerbaijan, he recalled that his latest meetings with Putin and Aliyev took place in Bishkek last month. He also spoke to the Russian president by phone the day before.
“The format is such that contacts with the president of Russia and the president of Azerbaijan will certainly take place. We will be in the same place today and tomorrow. No official meeting is planned. If it turns out that such a meeting is necessary, it may take place,” he said.
“Armenia has already faced such a threat”: response to Medvedev
People in Armenia continue to discuss Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev’s statement. He said that Armenia’s leadership had decided to change the country’s course and that this would not lead to anything good.
“The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” Medvedev said.
Journalists asked Pashinyan whether Armenia could face such a threat. He replied:
“Armenia has already faced a similar danger and situation. In September 2022, [during the Azerbaijani armed forces’ invasion of Armenia’s sovereign territory], the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations.”
The Collective Security Treaty Organisation is a military alliance led by Russia. Armenia is a member of the CSTO. Under the organisation’s charter, its allies had to provide military assistance to a member state, but that did not happen.
The Armenian prime minister could not explain why Medvedev was making such statements and threats:
“Following the same logic, someone else could say: ‘We do not want Armenia to turn into a “new Russia”, given that explosions can be heard in various parts of Russia.’ This is an unfortunate genre.”
He assured that Armenia would not turn into anything else and would instead become an even more independent state.
“Some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes”: on missing persons
Azerbaijan periodically demands that Armenia provide information about the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and the locations of their graves. President Ilham Aliyev repeated the demand at an international conference on missing persons in Baku.
According to Armenia’s prime minister, both sides should make joint efforts to establish the fate of missing people:
“We have stated that we are ready to cooperate. The problem is that some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes, including to generate hostile rhetoric and pursue other aims.”
According to figures Pashinyan presented, the whereabouts of around 1,000 people who went missing during wars since the 1990s remain unknown in Armenia.
He says the wording itself — “their whereabouts are unknown” — shows how little information the authorities have about these people:
“Some circles in Azerbaijan sometimes try to create the impression that we know where these people are and refuse to share the information. But that is not the case.”
Pashinyan believes the two sides should resolve the issue through cooperation and close this chapter. He said that in Bishkek, he and the Azerbaijani president also discussed stepping up joint efforts by the relevant commissions of the two countries.
