articles.title: Central Asia in an Emerging International Order: Shifting Strategic Partnerships with the GCC - Middle East Council on Global Affairs
articles.summary: Central Asia in an Emerging International Order: Shifting Strategic Partnerships with the GCC  Middle East Council on Global Affairs

source_detail.name: Middle East Council on Global Affairs

articles.full_text:
Rather than seeing a transfer of dominance from Russia to China, Central Asia is moving toward multipolarity: While Russia retains extensive security, economic, and human ties, China has become a structural component of the regional economy through trade, energy, and infrastructure. The deeper shift is that no single power monopolizes the region, creating greater room for maneuver for the Central Asian republics (C5) through multi-directional diplomacy.
The Gulf’s interest in Central Asia lies in investing capital and expertise without the geopolitical burdens affecting other powers: The GCC states are geographically distant from Central Asia and do not have a colonial legacy in the region; nor are they required to choose between competing powers. This allows them to pursue investments and partnerships without demanding political alignment.
Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar should coordinate to target their investments: Greater coordination would help transform potential competition into functional complementarity and strengthen the overall Gulf presence in the region.
Gulf strategy in Central Asia requires differentiated engagement with the five republics, rather than a uniform approach: The region’s business environments pose challenges that differ by country. Gulf investors must also account for the risk of secondary sanctions arising from ties with Russian entities, necessitating careful partner vetting and transaction structuring.
Central Asia is a vital strategic bridge connecting the Arab Gulf states to the wider Eurasian sphere. The region is re-emerging as a key arena of geopolitical competition and connectivity, driven by several concurrent shifts: the Russian-Ukrainian war, Moscow’s declining ability to monopolize influence across its former Soviet sphere, China’s economic rise, Europe’s search for alternative trade routes and energy sources, and intensifying global competition over energy, uranium, and critical minerals.
Central Asia’s geography further reinforces its strategic importance. Situated between Russia, China, Iran, Afghanistan, and the Caspian Sea, the region connects East Asia, Europe, South Asia, and the Arab world. Its five republics are home to approximately 84 million people and possess significant energy and mineral resources. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan together account for more than half of global uranium production, while the Middle Corridor—a transportation network linking China and Europe via the Caspian Sea—is gaining importance as an alternative trade route.1
Recent developments do not signal Russia’s withdrawal from Central Asia, nor Beijing’s replacement of Moscow as the dominant power. Russia retains an extensive network of security, economic, and human ties across the region, while China has become a structural component of its economy through trade, energy, infrastructure, and the Belt and Road Initiative. Meanwhile, Türkiye, the European Union, the United States, India, Iran, Japan, and South Korea have expanded their presence. The Central Asian republics have, to varying degrees, pursued multi-vector foreign policies to diversify their partnerships and avoid dependence on any single power. The most significant transformation, therefore, is not a shift in dominance from one power to another, but rather the declining ability of any single actor to monopolize the region, and the corresponding expansion of the Central Asian states’ room for geopolitical maneuver.
This gives Arab Gulf states an opportunity to move from scattered investments toward a strategic partnership with Central Asia. The needs of these two blocs are largely complementary: the Central Asian states need capital, technology, infrastructure, and new access points to global markets, while Gulf states are seeking to diversify their investments and food sources while strengthening their footing in renewable energy, critical minerals, supply chains, and Eurasian corridors. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar have each already begun building a tangible presence, particularly in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, in the energy, infrastructure, logistics, and technology sectors. Launched in 2022, the strategic dialogue between the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Central Asian states also provides an institutional framework on which to build.
The Gulf’s comparative advantage lies in its ability to provide capital, expertise, and access to markets without imposing a significant geopolitical cost. The Gulf states do not border Central Asia, have no modern colonial legacy in the region, and do not require their partners to choose between Russia, China, and the West. This paper therefore proposes transforming the Gulf’s existing presence into a more integrated regional strategy spanning energy, critical minerals, food security, railways, and logistics hubs. This strategy would also seek to connect Gulf ports with Central Asia and the Caspian Sea, positioning the Gulf as Central Asia’s southern gateway to global markets, while making the region the Gulf’s gateway to the rest of Eurasia.
The paper also recommends establishing a GCC consortium—led by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar—for projects of high geostrategic value. Such a consortium would be able to build flexible partnerships with major powers according to the requirements of each project, offering a link between the Gulf interests in Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Building this network would give the Gulf states greater geo-economic depth and additional deterrence and leverage vis-à-vis Iran, while keeping the door open to incorporating Tehran itself into a system of interests and corridors were it to commit to regional peace and stability.
The ultimate objective extends beyond increasing investment and trade. Rather, it amounts to transforming the Gulf’s presence at the heart of Eurasia into a new source of power, influence, and strategic agency in shaping the emerging international order.
Simply looking at maps can help explain much about international politics. A map of Central Asia reveals a vast landmass at the heart of the Eurasian continent and the intersection of four major arenas: the Russian and European spheres to the west and north, China and East Asia to the east, South Asia to the south, and the Arab world to the southwest. For millennia, this position has made it a point of connection and competition between different political, economic, and civilizational worlds.
Figure 1: Location of the Central Asian countries on the world map
It is therefore unsurprising that in the 19th century the region became the stage for the “Great Game” between the Russian and British empires.
Centuries earlier, the region had formed one of the most important sections of the Silk Road connecting East and West, as well as an arena for successive powers and empires. It was a center for rivalry between the pre-Islamic Sasanian and Byzantine empires,2 and later a theater for the conflicts waged by Arabs during the Umayyad and Abbasid periods against local powers in Transoxiana,3 eventually extending to rivalry with China’s Tang dynasty over influence in the region.4
Following the collapse of the Russian Empire and the Bolsheviks’ rise to power in October 1917, Soviet Russia was forced to relinquish the Baltic states, Finland, Poland, and western Ukraine under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. Yet between 1918 and 1924, it fought to retain control of Central Asia, even though the territories it had relinquished in Ukraine were culturally closer to Russia. This reflected the Bolsheviks’ recognition of the region’s geopolitical importance. Britain responded by supporting an insurgency in Central Asia known as the “Basmachi”5 movement, which brought together a range of local, nationalist, and Islamic currents seeking to remove the region, then referred to as “Western Turkestan,” from Soviet Russian control.6 Yet the region would remain under Soviet control throughout World War II and the Cold War. The Soviet-Afghan War from 1979-1989 dragged in a new superpower the other side of the world—the U.S.—further underscoring the region’s geopolitical importance at the global level.
After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Central Asia briefly receded from international attention, being largely viewed through the lens of maintaining security and stability. This manifested in a security treaty signed in 1992 at Russia’s initiative, which later developed into the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO)7, followed by the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO),8 formally established in 2001 with the participation of China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. Initially, the SCO focused on strengthening trust and security, while combating terrorism, separatism, and extremism, before expanding its political and economic scope.
Today, Central Asia comprises five republics, commonly referred to as the C5. Four have predominantly Turkic populations and languages: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, and Kyrgyzstan. In the document, the heads of state reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation between their countries within the framework of the United Nations and other international organizations of which they are members, and emphasized the importance of comprehensively and consistently developing multilateral cooperation, as well as implementing initiatives aimed at ensuring sustainable development, the well-being of their peoples, and long-term stability for the Central Asian states and Azerbaijan.

articles.title: Azerbaijan’s Sumgayit Industrial Park plans six new production buildings - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Azerbaijan’s Sumgayit Industrial Park plans six new production buildings  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Six new production buildings and supporting engineering infrastructure are planned at the Sumgayit Industrial Park in Azerbaijan.
According to information published on the Unified Internet Portal for Public Procurement, design and cost-estimate documentation will be prepared for the project.
The project will be implemented by the Economic Zones Development Agency (EZDA) under Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Economy and will cover a 2.29-hectare area allocated within the Sumgayit Industrial Park. The cost of the design and cost-estimate documentation services is 170,000 manats ($100,000).
The first phase envisages the construction of three production buildings. One building will have an area of 1,728 square meters, while the other two will each cover 1,920 square meters. Thus, the total area of the three buildings will amount to 5,568 square meters.
A further three production buildings, each covering 1,920 square meters, are planned in a subsequent phase. Once the second phase is completed, the total number of production buildings will reach six.
The project also includes the development of infrastructure required to support the new production facilities, including internal roads, electricity and water supply networks, sewerage systems, firefighting infrastructure and communications systems.
Internal roads will be built for the movement of freight vehicles, while technical roads, external lighting and landscaping are also planned.
Backup power systems will be installed to ensure reliable electricity supplies. These will include a diesel generator, an automatic backup power switching system and a dedicated area for the generator.
The production buildings will be equipped with drinking and technical water supply systems, domestic and stormwater sewerage systems, as well as firefighting water supply and fire protection systems. Telecommunications, internet and other low-voltage systems are also included in the project.
Video surveillance and access-control systems, as well as a checkpoint, are planned to improve security at the site. Sanitary facilities, general ventilation systems and other necessary utilities will also be provided in the production blocks.
The project will define the technical specifications of the production buildings. The buildings planned for the first phase are to be constructed using reinforced concrete structures and equipped with electricity, water, sewerage and fire safety systems. Specialized ventilation systems required for production purposes are expected to be installed separately by future tenants.
The design work will also cover site planning and leveling, engineering-geological and topographic surveys, preparation of a geological report, urban planning justification and a detailed master plan.
The project additionally envisages author supervision and the use of locally produced construction materials.
The Sumgayit Industrial Park was established by a decree signed by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev on December 21, 2011. Its main objectives are to create favorable conditions for the development of competitive industrial production based on innovative and high technologies, support entrepreneurship, contribute to the sustainable development of the non-oil sector and increase employment in industry.
The Sumgayit Industrial Park currently covers 640 hectares. Total investment in projects implemented at the park has reached $3.94 billion, while the number of permanent jobs planned to be created there stands at 6,134.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Uzbekistan and Germany agreed on German financing for eight projects in 2026–2027 during intergovernmental negotiations on financial and technical cooperation held in Tashkent on Oct. 7.

The negotiations were led by Uzbek Deputy Minister of Investments, Industry and Trade Akram Aliyev and Christiane Amari, head of the Division for Central Asia, Pakistan and Afghanistan at Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development.
The talks focused on priority areas of bilateral cooperation, including the green economy, vocational education, technical regulation, energy, public administration and social protection.

"Following the negotiations, the Protocol of Negotiations on Development Cooperation between the Government of the Republic of Uzbekistan and the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany was signed," the ministry said.
The protocol formalizes the results of the intergovernmental negotiations and provides a framework for further cooperation on development projects in Uzbekistan.
Additionally, the two sides reviewed areas where German technical expertise and financing could support Uzbekistan’s ongoing economic and institutional reforms, particularly in green development, energy, vocational training and public administration.
The negotiations form part of Uzbekistan’s broader efforts to expand cooperation with European partners and attract financing and technical expertise for projects supporting sustainable economic development.

articles.title: Sadyr Japarov strengthens partnership with Azerbaijan - new chapter in relations - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Sadyr Japarov strengthens partnership with Azerbaijan - new chapter in relations  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov took part in the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan on October 8. The meeting was held at the Awaza complex in Turkmenistan. The summit was also attended by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan.
Sadyr Japarov’s speech at the meeting shows that Bishkek sees cooperation with Azerbaijan not only as a political partnership, but also as an opportunity to expand practical ties in trade, industry, transport, the digital economy and tourism. Several of the initiatives are directly linked to strengthening economic ties between Central Asia, and the South Caucasus.
One of the key proposals from the Kyrgyz side was the creation of a unified electronic trading platform for Central Asia and Azerbaijan.
"In this regard, we propose creating a unified electronic trading platform for Central Asia and Azerbaijan. This would provide consumers and businesses with broader access to goods produced in the countries of the region," Sadyr Japarov said.
According to him, the development of e-commerce should go hand in hand with stronger industrial cooperation. Kyrgyzstan proposes that the governments of the countries in the region identify specific mutually beneficial projects in agricultural processing, light industry, construction materials and logistics, including the participants, sources of financing and implementation timelines.
Such an approach could create a basis for moving from growing mutual trade to more sustainable industrial cooperation. If such projects are implemented, Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan could have additional opportunities to promote each other’s products, while Central Asian companies could use Azerbaijani infrastructure to access the South Caucasus and other international markets.
Transport remains one of the most important elements of the emerging regional connection. Sadyr Japarov proposed that the transport authorities of the countries, together with carriers, develop practical solutions for unified freight tariffs, coordinated schedules, shorter waiting times and digital cargo tracking.
"Our focus should be on measurable results: reducing delivery costs and travel time. At the same time, every country should have the opportunity to fully participate in regional transport projects and receive economic benefits from them," the Kyrgyz president said.
In this context, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project is particularly important. Its further integration with routes through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan could create an additional land-sea connection between China, the countries of the region and South Caucasus markets. For Kyrgyzstan, this could provide more options for reaching foreign markets, while for Azerbaijan it could strengthen its role as a transport link between Central Asia and wider international routes.
Trade figures also show that economic ties between the two countries already have a basis for further growth. In 2025, trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan amounted to $77.17 million, increasing about 1.9 times compared with 2024. Azerbaijan’s imports from Kyrgyzstan reached $53.75 million, while Azerbaijan’s exports to Kyrgyzstan amounted to $23.42 million.
In January-July 2026, the situation changed. Azerbaijan’s exports to Kyrgyzstan reached $30.03 million, exceeding the full-year 2025 figure by 28.2 percent, while imports from Kyrgyzstan amounted to $4.03 million. As a result, Azerbaijan’s trade surplus with Kyrgyzstan reached about $26 million during the period. This trend creates room for further growth in mutual supplies and a wider range of goods.
The Azerbaijan-Kyrgyz Development Fund is another important basis for investment cooperation. In July 2026, its capital was increased from $100 million to $200 million. At the same time, three joint projects were opened and eight more initiatives were launched, creating a financial basis for moving toward larger industrial projects.
Tourism is another important area of bilateral relations. In July, the Azerbaijani-built five-star Baku Resort & Spa was opened in the village of Kara-Oy on Lake Issyk-Kul. The project covers more than 17 hectares and includes 111 rooms and 10 cottages. It can accommodate 330 guests and is expected to create 255 jobs at the initial stage. Projects like this not only develop tourism infrastructure but also create additional opportunities for people-to-people and business ties.
Against this background, cooperation between Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan is gradually moving beyond individual projects. The political foundation of relations is also becoming stronger. The two countries have previously signed a Treaty on Allied Relations. Kyrgyz Ambassador to Azerbaijan Maksat Mamytkanov said earlier that following Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s state visit to Kyrgyzstan, relations had reached a higher level of interstate cooperation and that ties were expected to become more active in all areas.
Further cooperation could develop in several directions. One could be an increase in mutual trade through a wider range of goods and new industrial projects. Another could involve the gradual creation of a common digital and logistics environment, including e-commerce, digital documents, cargo tracking and coordinated tariffs.
Another possible scenario is closer integration of Kyrgyzstan’s transport projects with routes through the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan. In this case, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway could become part of a wider regional transport system connecting Central Asia with Azerbaijan and international markets.
Investment and tourism could also support further cooperation. The increased capital of the Azerbaijan-Kyrgyz Development Fund could provide financing for new projects, while joint promotion of tourism routes could strengthen contacts between the people of the two countries. Environmental cooperation also remains a possible area, including the sustainable use of natural resources and the protection of glaciers and mountain ecosystems.
